messages.subject_clean: Various obsCovs errors in creating unmarkedFrameGMM
messages.body_plain:
I have what I think is a fairly straightforward problem with formatting my obsCovs correctly for creation of an unmarkedFrameGMM.

I'm using point counts of birds at ~840 sites with 1-3 visits at each site and 3 subintervals for each visit. The data is formatted for each species with rows of each site and columns of each visit and subinterval (i.e., 1-1, 1-2, 1-3, 2-1, etc.). The siteCovs is similar with rows of each site and columns of different variables (canopy, chaparral, etc.). Those two pieces seem to fit fine with the data loaded as a matrix and the siteCovs loaded as a data frame.

Now the obsCovs--I initially created a table with with rows of site-visit-subinterval and columns of the variables (noise, surveyor, Julian date, and minutes past sunrise) because that's what it seemed the help file was telling me. I simply assigned that table to the object obsCovs and when building my unmarkedFrameGMM used obsCovs=obsCovs. That returned the error that
"invalid class "unmarkedFrame" object: obsCovData does not have M*obsNum rows."
I then tried entering it as the help file later suggests by setting occasion equal to my data:
obsCovs=list(occasion=obsCovs)
which gave the error:
"At least one matrix in obsCovs has incorrect number of dimensions"
Finally I tried importing a csv for each observation covariate separately and in the same form as the data and the siteCovs (with rows of site and columns of visit-subinterval). I made a list of those (as suggested by a previous post in this group) and input them in the same two ways I tried previously with the same error messages. I've tried several permutations of these methods and I keep getting the same two error messages.

So I guess my big question is can someone clarify in what form my obsCovs need to be in order for R to be satisfied? The help file is extremely unclear and I am completely new to R.

Thanks!

Hi Caitlin, if you look at obsCovs(umfGMM1) in the example for unmarkedMultFrame, you'll see that the single covariate "occasion" is ultimately formatted as an MTJ vector by the umf function.  But when you create the umf you can either specify the obsCovs covariates in long format (single MTJ vector) as a data frame, or wide format (M by TJ matrix) as a list.  You cannot specify the long format as a list.  I think most folks work with the wide format since it is easier to envision, but unmarked uses the long format during model fitting for increased speed.  Here are the options:

# wide format

occasions <- data.frame(matrix(rep(1:(J*T), each=n), n, J*T))

...obsCovs=list(occasion=occasions)

# long format
occasions <- as.vector(t(data.frame(matrix(rep(1:(J*T), each=n), n, J*T))))
...obsCovs=data.frame(occasion=occasions)

Understanding the structure of a list, data frame, array, matrix, etc. is a tricky but important part of R (and programming in general).  There are many webpages with helpful explanations.

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Sarah Frey found a bug in pcountOpen that causes problems when the covariates of gamma, omega, or iota vary among primary periods but not among sites. If you use this type of covariate, you should notice that your AIC values are extremely different (eg greater than an order of magnitude larger) than models without the covariate.

This issue will not arise if any of the gamma/omega/iota covariates in the model vary among sites.

I will try to fix this as soon as I can, but in the meantime, do not rely on models in which the covariates vary among primary periods but not among sites.

Richard

Hi Danielle, what was your maximum value for K?  This should be set to a value higher than is biologically possible.

Your model was structured as an "effects" parameterization, whereby the differences between each year and the baseline year (intercept) are estimated. Therefore, if you want the mean value for a given year, you have to add the intercept to each year's effect estimate.  You could rerun that model with gammaformula= ~year-1 to remove the intercept and get a "means" parameterization, where each estimate is now the mean for the given factor (e.g., year).

Hi Danielle,

If your data suggest that p was very low, then the model will find it plausible that N was very high, and you will therefore need to set K to a large value. If you do not have robust design data, the model can easily mistake heterogeneity in the abundance dynamics as evidence that p was low.  So try to explain as much of the variation as possible using covariates. If you still have convergence problems, then you probably don't have enough data to estimate the parameters well, and you should consider collecting additional data using the robust design or other sampling methods that provide direct information about the detection process.

It appears as though you coded year as a continuous variable and not a factor. Was that your intention?

Richard

Jeff

Greetings all,

I'm interested in the detection process underlying some count data and not in the abundance/state process. I've used an offset (log of known abundance) to predict abundance (and several highly predictive detection covariates), but I'm still getting unreasonably high estimates of abundance due to the intercept (I tried the NB mixture, but P was the most realistic). Is there a way to either (1) remove the intercept (attempted; consistently crashes R) or (2) assign a known abundance vector similar to knownOcc in an occu model?

Thanks, as always, to the unmarked developers and community!

Giancarlo

I was hoping to copy an AICc table from a software program into a manuscript and realized the table actually was displaying an AIC table.  To convert AIC to AICc the software requests the effective sample size.  My guess is that the effective sample size is the number of sites.  Effective sample size seemingly is only mentioned once in the MacKenzie et al. (2006) book.  That is in the context of occupancy modeling and it mentions that number of sites is used unless sites are not independent.  I did not find the term 'effective sample size' in the Royle 2004 paper, but might have overlooked it.

I did find an post here from 2010 in which it was suggested to just stick with AIC, albeit that may have been for a different model.

In my case, I have a fairly large number of sites, ~ 700 - 3500.  So, I doubt there is any real difference between AIC and AICc, but I wanted to ask.

Thanks for any suggestions.

Mark

hi Mark,

 I don't think it's safe to say that effective sample size is the number of sites.... I don't think there's a clear answer to this question so far as computing AICc goes.   I guess there's more information about detection covariates coming from the temporal replication and vice versa for the abundance covariates. But the likelihood is the same for both effects and so it wouldn't make sense for them to have a different effective sample size.

 I recommend not using AICc for any hierarchical model in which sample size has no clear meaning.

 Other opinions on this?

regards
andy

messages.body_plain:
For some data types (excuse the MARK-ism), the effective sample size is relatively straightforward (to the degree, at least, that there is a consensus as to how to calculate it). For example, for known fate (simplest model), it is simply the total number of 'exposure days', since each interval is considered independent of any other interval. For nest survival, number of days known alive + 1 for the interval where nest dies. For CJS and similar data types like simple multi-state, the number of releases and re-releases. Simple chain binomials and related things.

Where things get ugly is when you have 'interesting but annoying' flavours of parameters. As Gary noted in his response to the PhiDot discussion Murray refers to (http://www.phidot.org/forum/viewtopic.php?f=1&t=914), [note in particular the stuff in italics...]

 "...early on, the effective sample size (in MARK) was always taken as the number of Bernoulli trials. So, for the CJS model, the number of animals released and re-released is taken as the effective sample size, because these releases form Bernoulli trials. Similarly for dead recoveries and known fate data types. When this philosophy got questioned was with the models that had different types of parameters. First were the robust design models, and later the occupancy models. Clearly in the simple occupancy models, psi has a different sample size than p. psi is based on the number of patches, whereas p is based on the number of visits to patches..."

In other words, for occupancy, robust design (and probably everything based on permutations or hybrids of same), there is no consensus on what constitutes the effective sample size. As such, my general recommendation for folks is: use AIC, and as an ad hoc bit of comfort assessment, try different values for effective sample size, using the standard AIC formulation, and see if its going to make much difference. If not, then AIC is no doubt safe. If you have a smallish sample, by some criterion, then perhaps there is reason to be concerned.

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I have a general question regarding how best to parameterise a multi-season occupancy model.

The objective of the model is to assess the relative importance of changing climate and habitat amount on extinction and colonization rates of a bird species over a 20-year period, while accounting for detection probabilities. At each site, and for each year of detection data, I have covariates describing amount of habitat and a heat stress index (yearlySiteCovs). These covariates are both space and time-varying. We also included time-dependence in the extinction component by including 'year' as a factor to examine whether there was a trend over time. In the final model, considering only extinction probabilities for illustrative purposes, this resulted in a single beta estimate for each covariate of habitat and heat stress, and a year factor for each of the 20 years.

I found this post, and am now concerned that including time (here 'year' as a factor) and time-varying covariates may be problematic:
http://www.phidot.org/forum/viewtopic.php?f=1&t=2363&p=7377&hilit=+temporal+variation+#p7377

My specific questions include:
1) Is it a problem to include both time-varying covariates and time (i.e. 'year') as a factor ? As per the phidot post, the answer to this seems like a 'yes'....and this can result in over-fitting. I would really like to better understand why this is case.

2) For a multi-season occupancy model that includes time-varying covariates, is it possible to get at the variation explained due to temporal vs spatial changes in covariates, and what is the best way to parameterise the model to identify these sources of variation? In a single year model, a covariate describing, for example, % habitat amount for each primary sampled site, and the resulting beta estimates would to my understanding be addressing spatial variation across the sampled sites. In a multi-season occupancy model which includes time-varying covariates on the extinction and colonization terms, do these beta estimates represent spatial or temporal variation? If I included a year as a factor on both extintion/colonization terms, would there be no temporal variation left to be explained by the time-varying covariates of habitat and climate?  I might be missing something obvious here, but any ideas, resources, etc, much appreciated.

I have been working with the R package unmarked, so am posting it here, but happy to send over to another list-serve. Huge thanks to everyone.

Ilona

Hi Ilona,

There is a general issue that I think you hit on; without some decomposing of covariates, parameters for a spatiotemporally-varying covariate (say, precipitation) could (depending on how long and over how large an area is studied) be influenced heavily by one "dimension" and only slightly by the other; but we wouldn't know without further digging (despite the certainty I've sometimes seen in discussion sections =) ).

Without additional detail, it's hard to say if including factor(year) would be over-fitting in your model. If most of the variation is over time (for example, temperature in a small study area), then yes. If spread over space and time, then inclusion of factor(year) would result in a parameter estimate (say, for % habitat) that is addressing the spatial variation (some good simulations showing this in a different context: van de Pol, M., and J. Wright. 2009. Animal Behaviour 77:753-758).

To digress a bit, and sticking with the precipitation example, the balance of the variation is over space in a large area like the western U.S., and there's an argument (in this case) for using site-specific means to address the spatial variation in this covariate and anomalies to address temporal variation. BTW, this is standard stuff among climatologists, less so among ecologists! =) In this example (from my experience), other covariates *may* become redundant; for example elevation (cor with precip means) and factor(year) (cor with anomalies).

- G

Giancarlo, when you say spatial means vs. temporal anomalies, it sounds like the effects in one dimension (space) are treated as fixed while variation in the other dimension (time) is treated as random.  It seems with enough replication you could specify variation as random in both dimensions, and then the distinction is not necessary. I think you make an excellent point that just because variation in a dimension is possible and was recorded, does not mean the model will be able to fit such complexity.  And the variation can be very unbalanced, depending on the scales at each dimension, affecting your ability to make certain inferences. This limits the complexity of temporal relationships that can be modeled, unless there is enough spatio-temporal variation.
